description:
With Valeri Ponzo; Day 2 of our 3-day Thanksgiving holiday trip to the eastern Panhandle.

Our itinerary for Day 2 was:

0655-1008 CST: Chipola River Water Management Area (Calhoun County; return trip from yesterday)

1016-1118 CST: Altha Park (Calhoun County)

1122-1153 CST: Mount Olive Cemetery Road (Calhoun County)

1245-1304 CST: lunch at the Blountstown Subway (Calhoun County)

1335-1343 CST: Willis Bridge Park (Calhoun County; 1 species!)

1400-1506 CST: Chipola River Boat Ramp (Calhoun County)

1615-1708 CST: Sam Atkins Park (Calhoun County; we got rained out)

1845 CST: we checked into the Apalachicola Bay Inn (Franklin County). We ate at a rather pricey restaurant in Apalachicola, where all food was served in Styrofoam containers and plasticware, which was all thrown into the trash when we were finished; weird. 

We barely saw the sun on any of the three days; most photographs were taken under gloomy skies, which meant that I often had to boost the light saturation to get a usable image, even if the image ended up looking washed-out.

Val and I have set a goal of attaining 50 or more bird species in each of Florida's 67 counties (Val has reached or exceeded this total in 57 counties, while I have reached or exceeded 50 species in 56 counties). Calhoun County was our primary target this trip; we each started the trip with 14 species. Owing to Val's much-better hearing than mine, Val ended this day with 51 species, while I ended up with 45.

From 1030-1230, I conducted a stationary watch from the southern mound, the first time in several years that I have done this (there were no Mother Truckers in the Preserve today!). On April 16th, 2025, beachgoers began reporting landbirds washing up on beaches from (at least) Panama City, Florida, westward to (at least) Fort Morgan, Alabama. Photos and descriptions indicated these were typical trans-Gulf neotropical migrants. These are birds that undertake a perilous crossing of over 450 miles of open water of the Gulf of Mexico, from the northern Yucatan (and points south) to the northern Gulf Coast from northwest Florida to Southeast Texas. Typically, migrants leave at dusk on south winds, and make the crossing of the Gulf of Mexico in anywhere from 12 to 20 hours, depending on species and trailing wind speed. Under ideal conditions they fly over the coast and land well inland. However, when birds encounter adverse weather over the Gulf, the flight can be delayed, and tired birds that make it “fall-out” along the coast, the timing depending upon various conditions. On the morning of April 16, a fall-out developed along the northwest Florida coast and extended at least as far as Fort Morgan, Alabama, where spectacular numbers of migrants were grounded. The timing of arrival was unusual. A dawn arrival suggests that these birds had left the Yucatan and other jump off points not at dusk on April 15, but rather at dusk on April 14, and had been struggling over the gulf for about 36 hours into strong northwesterly winds. 
It has been widely demonstrated by observations from boats and offshore platforms that during such conditions, many trans-gulf migrants burn up their fat reserves during the crossing and perish at sea. Under the right conditions bodies wash up on beaches. I walked 2 miles from east to west the evening of April 17 into the Fort Pickens unit of Gulf Islands National Seashore through a heavy visitor use area, including a designated dog beach. I found 22 dead trans-gulf migrants: 7 Red-eyed Vireos (6 photographed); 2 Gray Catbirds; 2 Barn Swallows; 1 Ovenbird; 6 Scarlet Tanagers (5 photographed); 1 Rose-breasted Grosbeak; and 3 Indigo Buntings. All of these species were seen in numbers at Fort Pickens on the morning of the 16th.

description:
With Don Fraser, Clint Gibson, Shelley Rutkin, and Liz Childress; a successful chase of two rare bees. We found Colletes banksi pollening on Dahoon Holly (Ilex cassine) -- a new food plant -- and we found several Melissodes mitchelli, the star of the show. According to Clint (who knows these things), mitchelli had not been identifiable photographed in the wild previously! It all started on 12 April 2025, when Don, Clint, and I participated in the Annuteliga Hammock butterfly count. During the count, I saw a bee gathering pollen from a prickly pear cactus. I took one cell-phone photograph then the bee was gone. Later, I showed Clint the photo, and he said that could be a real good bee, Melissodes mitchelli, which is a Florida endemic, is exclusive to prickly pear pollen ("oligolectic"), and is known from just a few records, all of them specimens. It turns out that Don had photographed probably the same bee last year at Chassahowitzka Wildlife and Environmental Area on a trip with me and Alice Herden. Then, Cliff and his wife found and collected a male Melissodes mitchelli (Clint has permits ...) at Starkey Wilderness Preserve on 17 April 2025. So the stage was set for this day at Chassahowitzka. Clint found and captured (but did not collect) a Melissodes mitchelli, which we all photographed before Clint released it. We started out on Rattlesnake Camp Road and then drove Scrub Island Road. Finally, we drove 3 Bridge Road to the sandhills area at the northern edge of the property. I took my first photographs at 1055 and my last at 1539. The weather at the start was sunny, 84 degrees ("feels like" 85), and with SW winds at 9 MPH.

These are my camera photographs, which are given a random circle at Rattlesnake Camp Road and 3 Bridge Road, and the beginning time of 1055.
